name: Lateral osteotomy (nasal)

lead: A lateral nasal osteotomy is a controlled cut in the nasal bone made during rhinoplasty so that the bony vault can be moved. Surgeons use it to narrow a wide nasal bridge, straighten a crooked nose, or close the gap left after a bony hump is removed.

The appearance payoff is a nose that looks slimmer and more aligned, which affects overall facial balance. Reviews of rhinoplasty describe osteotomies as common but demanding, with technique choices such as chisels or powered saws affecting bruising and swelling.

paras: It is performed by a surgeon within a rhinoplasty, through small internal incisions or through the skin, using osteotomes or powered instruments. Bruising and swelling afterwards are typical, and the nose is taped and splinted.

Reviews warn that poorly planned osteotomies can create step deformities, an inverted-V, a pinched or saddle nose, and that over-narrowing can block the airway. Percutaneous approaches have been criticized for possible visible scars. It is a surgical procedure that belongs with a qualified surgeon.

chain: Controlled cuts along the nasal bone
The bony vault is narrowed or realigned
angle.text: Osteotomy is how surgeons change the bony part of the nose when the shape comes from bone, not cartilage. It is used to narrow a wide bridge, straighten a crooked one and close the open roof after hump reduction.

lead: A lateral osteotomy is a controlled break made along the side of the nasal bones during rhinoplasty so the bony vault can be moved. Reviews describe the main indications as correcting a deviated nose, narrowing the bony vault and closing an open roof after a large hump has been removed.[1][2]

The aim for appearance is a bridge that looks narrower, straighter and better aligned with the rest of the face. Osteotomies are named by location: lateral, intermediate, medial and superior or transverse, and may be done through the inside of the nose (endonasal) or through the skin (percutaneous).[2]

Surgical reviews say osteotomies should not be done routinely, because the nose needs to be analysed precisely first to avoid deformities.[1] Research comparing instruments and approaches, such as powered saws, piezoelectric devices and percutaneous versus internal cuts, has focused on bruising, swelling and visible scarring.[3][4][5]
infobox: Wide bony vault, crooked nose, open roof

paras: A nasal osteotomy modifies the bony part of the nose. The ideal result is described as precise, predictable and reproducible, with minimal soft-tissue trauma and complications.[2] Review articles cover the anatomy, the paths of lateral, intermediate, medial and superior cuts, timing, and instrument choice.[2]

Common indications are closing an open roof after hump reduction, straightening a crooked nose and narrowing a wide bony vault.[2] Lateral osteotomies and grafts are described as crucial in preventing open-roof abnormalities after hump removal.[6]

Powered instruments have seen greater use and are felt by some surgeons to improve on traditional methods, and osteotomy sequence can significantly affect final results. A comparison of continuous and perforating osteotomy showed a difference in bruising and swelling rather than effectiveness.[3]

A French review lists step deformity, inverted-V, pinched nose and saddle nose among deformities that can result, and notes that over-narrowed bones can obstruct the airway.[1] The percutaneous technique has been criticized for possible visible scarring, a point examined in a randomized, blinded study.[5]

Randomized trials have compared a powered micro-saw with a conventional osteotome in 60 septorhinoplasty patients, percutaneous with internal osteotomy for visible scars, and piezosurgery with conventional osteotomy for post-rhinoplasty morbidity.[4][5][7] These studies address instruments and complications, not whether the procedure is desirable.
